Your best bet if you don't want to spend hundreds of dollars having your set calibrated is to Google the model number of your set with the word picture settings after it. CNET usually can provide good settings of TVs that were professionally calibrated and there are countless other sources but usually they will be pretty close to the same settings. In almost all cases you will want your picture set to MOVIE/THX/PURE mode. Often times until your eyes adjust to these settings you will think the picture looks dull and yellow. If you compare calibrated settings to what you are probably currently using you will think the calibrated settings are terrible in comparison . You are very wrong. Give it a few hours, let your eyes adjust and you will start to understand why these settings are so much better.

This will explain a little more detail: Movie directors try to affect an audience as much with the look of the film as with the performance of the actors, the art direction, the musical score, and all the other things that go into making a film. They are not trying to faithfully reproduce real life as is the goal of the nature photographer or the director of a major network sporting event like a football game.

Sometimes this manipulation goes pretty far. The Godfather movies were deliberately shot with a somewhat sepia tone and lots of visible film grain to give them a more "period" look. Spielberg deliberately "flared" the fires on the Normandy beach scenes in Saving Private Ryan because the original newsreel films of the landing had the same effect because the film stock got wet on the day. In both cases there was a hue and cry from dvd buyers over supposed defects in the dvd transfers and some even suspected their equipment was malfunctionning.

The director will deviate from a standard baseline to achieve the desired look by manipulating color temp, contrast, saturation, etc. If the equipment used to display the movie, whether in a theater or at home, is not set to the same standard baseline, the film won't look the way the director meant for it to look.

This is why it's important to have a set calibrated in at least one picture mode to as close to that baseline as possible. Deviating from this by pumping up the white level, oversharpenning until there are white ghosts at all contrast boundaries, and bluing whites to little old lady hair color standards is as bad as colorizing old movies, cropping the picture to fit a tv screen, digitally removing film grain, or overdubbing certain dialogue so as not to offend the prudish among network tv viewers or airline passengers.

Having that accurate baseline is also kinda cool as it can reveal the differences between different color processes over the years--the old 3 strip technicolor movies like Wizard of Oz or the 1938 Robin Hood had a definite special look to them that doesn't show on an uncalibrated display.

The end goal is to see the picture as the producer/artist intended you to.
